title: Building Capacity
author: Nick Hart
summary: Hart addresses a practical school-leadership problem: what to do when a leadership team shrinks because a senior leader departs, is delayed in being replaced, or has to pick up more teaching load. He frames the answer around three distinct kinds of capacity -- physical (headcount), organisational (how well the team as a whole learns and what it collectively attends to), and intellectual (the expertise of individual leaders). On organisational capacity, he leans on Dylan Wiliam's idea that effective leadership means stopping people doing good things so they have room for better things, and asks leaders to audit how much of their collective time goes to maintenance versus improvement. On intellectual capacity, he breaks expertise into enabling beliefs, domain-specific knowledge, context-specific knowledge, and stage of ego development, and offers a concrete tactic for each -- from storytelling to reinforce beliefs, to deliberately disruptive conversations with other leaders to advance ego development. The piece ends with a compact summary checklist tying each capacity type to specific actions a leadership team can take.
points: Hart distinguishes three types of leadership capacity a school can build after losing a senior leader: physical (headcount), organisational (collective learning and attention), and intellectual (individual expertise).

He cites Dylan Wiliam's claim that effective leadership largely consists of stopping teachers doing good things so they have time for even better things, and applies the same logic to leadership teams' own workload.
Expertise is broken into four components -- enabling beliefs, domain-specific knowledge, context-specific knowledge, and stage of ego development -- each requiring a different building strategy.
Hart argues ego development specifically requires 'disruptive experiences,' such as talking with other leaders about shared problems to expose different ways of thinking.
He frames adding headcount as the costliest way to rebuild capacity, one that may or may not be vindicated depending on whether the right people end up in the right roles.
quotes: In each case here, there might be fewer people available to do the leadership work a school needs. How might we go about increasing leadership capacity in this situation? Let's look at physical capacity, organisational capacity and intellectual capacity.

Schools improve when outcomes for children are better, whether those outcomes are academic or pastoral and a range of sub categories for each. And there can be no improvement to outcomes for children without the adults collectively becoming more expert.

Dylan Wiliam has argued that the essence of effective leadership is stopping teachers doing good things, to give them more time to spend on even better things. This is a conundrum for us all; we might think that there are useless practices that we can cull to free up time and attention for better things but there are probably less of these than we think.

Organisational capacity is probably dependent on the intellectual capacity of the individual leaders. More expert individuals, I'd argue, will contribute more to organisational capacity. So we can add capacity by developing the expertise of individual leaders.

How might we develop our ego? In short, we need disruptive experiences. Simply talking with other leaders about common problems to expose different ways of thinking provides a useful disruptive experience.
